Name: Diaphragmatic breathing with relaxed abdominal expansion
Purpose: Practise relaxed breathing and reduce unnecessary guarding before movement.
Exercise type: Breathing and respiratory control
Targeted musclegroups: Respiratory muscles; deep trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: diaphragma; musculi intercostales externi; musculi intercostales interni; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis
Equipment and environment: A mat, carpet or firm bed; two small pillows may support the knees.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with knees bent and feet flat, or sit supported with both feet on the floor. Rest one hand on the lower ribs and one on the upper chest.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Let the shoulders drop. 2) Breathe in gently through the nose and feel the lower ribs widen into the sides of the hands. 3) Breathe out slowly through relaxed lips. 4) Repeat without forcing the abdomen outward.
Range and direction: The lower ribs and abdomen should move softly; do not try to make the chest completely still.
Breathing: Breathe slowly and continuously; never hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: Take 5–10 breaths for 1–3 rounds, resting about 30 seconds between rounds.
Expected sensation: A mild sense of relaxation or gentle movement of the ribs is expected; dizziness means the breaths are too large or too fast.
Regression: Use a seated version or breathe normally without trying to expand a particular area.
Progression: Practise the same breathing while walking, lifting or performing a strengthening exercise.
Common errors and corrections: Shrugging the shoulders—let them hang; forcing a large breath—make each breath smaller; pulling the abdomen in hard—allow it to move.
Evidence category: Breathing and self-management
Evidence strength: Not established as a standalone treatment; used as a practical preparation and comfort skill.
Source: Technique context: Kisner et al., Therapeutic Exercise, 8th ed. Efficacy is not inferred from the technique source.
Name: Supine abdominal brace
Purpose: Practise a gentle trunk contraction while keeping normal breathing.
Exercise type: Isometric strength and motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Deep trunk stabilisers; abdominal muscles
Targeted specific muscles: musculus transversus abdominis; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; optional folded towel under the head.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet hip-width apart and arms resting by your sides. Keep the neck relaxed.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in. 2) As you breathe out, gently tighten around the abdomen as if preparing for a light touch. 3) Keep the ribs, pelvis and buttocks relaxed. 4) Release gradually while continuing to breathe.
Range and direction: Use only enough tension to feel mild support; do not press the lower back hard into the floor.
Breathing: Breathe in before the brace and breathe out slowly while holding it; do not hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 5–8 holds of 5–10 seconds, resting 20–30 seconds between holds.
Expected sensation: Mild abdominal effort is expected; cramping, pelvic-floor pressure or breathlessness is not.
Regression: Use a 20–30% effort or practise one breath at a time without holding a timed contraction.
Progression: Maintain the gentle brace while moving one heel or arm.
Common errors and corrections: Maximal tightening—use less effort; holding the breath—count slow breaths; lifting the ribs—relax the chest.
Evidence category: Low-load trunk control
Evidence strength: Part of motor-control exercise; the individual brace has not been shown to be uniquely superior.
Source: Saragiotto et al. 2016; Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Bent-knee fallout
Purpose: Train trunk control while one hip moves.
Exercise type: Motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Hip abductors; deep trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus medius; musculus gluteus minimus; musculus tensor fasciae latae; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat about hip-width apart, arms beside you and pelvis in a comfortable middle position.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in. 2) Let one knee slowly move outward a few centimetres. 3) Keep the movement smooth and return the knee to centre. 4) Alternate sides.
Range and direction: The knee moves; the pelvis may move slightly but should not roll heavily toward the moving side.
Breathing: Breathe normally; exhale as the knee moves outward and inhale as it returns.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 6–12 repetitions per side, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort around the abdomen and hip is expected; do not force the knee toward the floor.
Regression: Use a smaller outward movement or support the knee with a pillow.
Progression: Move farther, slow the return or add a gentle brace.
Common errors and corrections: Pelvis rolling—shorten the range; knee dropping quickly—move more slowly; feet too wide—bring them closer to hip width.
Evidence category: Motor-control and hip control
Evidence strength: Reasonable exercise-category option; direct evidence for this exact variation is indirect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Heel slide
Purpose: Coordinate hip movement with low-load trunk control.
Exercise type: Motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Hip flexors; abdominal muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus iliacus; musculus psoas major; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; optional pillow under the head.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with both knees bent and feet flat. Keep arms by the sides and choose a comfortable pelvic position.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Gently prepare the abdomen. 2) Slide one heel slowly away until the leg is partly straight. 3) Slide it back without pushing hard through the other foot. 4) Alternate sides.
Range and direction: The leg lengthens along the floor; do not lift the heel unless the exercise is progressed.
Breathing: Breathe continuously; exhale while sliding away and inhale as the heel returns.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 5–10 repetitions per side, with 30–60 seconds rest.
Expected sensation: Mild abdominal and hip effort is expected; avoid sharp back or groin pain.
Regression: Slide only a few centimetres or keep one foot still and practise the motion separately.
Progression: Slide farther, pause at the far point or combine with an opposite-arm reach.
Common errors and corrections: Back arching—shorten the slide; pushing through the stationary foot—relax it; rushing—use a three-second slide.
Evidence category: Low-load trunk and hip coordination
Evidence strength: Part of structured exercise; no evidence that this exact exercise is superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Dead-bug heel tap
Purpose: Build trunk endurance while the legs move away from the body.
Exercise type: Strength and motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Hip flexors; abdominal muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus iliopsoas; musculus rectus femoris; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with hips and knees bent as if sitting in a chair; arms may rest by the sides or point upward. Keep the head supported.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in. 2) Lower one heel toward the floor. 3) Tap lightly or stop before contact. 4) Return the leg and repeat on the other side.
Range and direction: Move only as far as you can without straining or forcefully flattening the back.
Breathing: Exhale while lowering the heel and inhale as it returns; breathe normally between repetitions.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 5–10 per side, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild abdominal effort is expected; the exercise should not cause sharp or spreading symptoms.
Regression: Keep the working knee closer to the chest or keep the other foot supported.
Progression: Add arm movement, increase the leg lever or use a slow three-second lowering phase.
Common errors and corrections: Lower back arching—reduce the range; neck tension—support the head; breath-holding—pause and reset.
Evidence category: Trunk endurance and motor control
Evidence strength: Motor-control exercise is probably beneficial versus minimal intervention, but this variation is not individually validated.
Source: Saragiotto et al. 2016; Verville et al. 2023.
Name: Dead-bug with opposite arm and leg
Purpose: Progress trunk control to coordinated arm-and-leg movement.
Exercise type: Strength and motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Abdominal muscles; hip flexors; shoulder flexors; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus transversus abdominis; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus iliopsoas; musculus rectus femoris; musculus deltoideus; musculus pectoralis major; musculus serratus anterior
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with hips and knees bent and arms pointing toward the ceiling, or use the heel-tap version first.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in. 2) Slowly reach one arm overhead while extending the opposite leg. 3) Stop before the ribs lift or back arches. 4) Return both limbs and change sides.
Range and direction: Use a shorter arm or leg lever if control is lost; the movement is slow and symmetrical.
Breathing: Exhale during the reach and inhale as you return; never hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 5–8 repetitions per side, resting 45–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the abdomen and hips is expected; do not chase a large range.
Regression: Move one limb at a time or keep the leg bent.
Progression: Lengthen the lever, add a 2–3-second pause or hold a very light object in the hands.
Common errors and corrections: Ribs lifting—shorten the reach; pelvis rocking—reduce the leg range; rushing—count two seconds out and two seconds back.
Evidence category: Motor-control and trunk endurance
Evidence strength: Reasonable part of a progressive exercise programme; not shown to be uniquely superior.
Source: Saragiotto et al. 2016; Verville et al. 2023.
Name: Pelvic tilts
Purpose: Explore comfortable pelvic and lower-back movement without searching for one perfect posture.
Exercise type: Mobility
Targeted musclegroups: Trunk flexors and extensors; pelvic stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus abdominis; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus gluteus maximus
Equipment and environment: Mat, carpet or a chair for the standing version.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with knees bent, or stand with your back lightly against a wall and feet slightly forward.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Slowly tip the pelvis so the lower back moves a little toward the floor or wall. 2) Return through the middle position. 3) Gently move the pelvis the other way. 4) Repeat in a small, comfortable arc.
Range and direction: Use a small range; the movement should be smooth rather than a forceful flattening or arching.
Breathing: Breathe normally throughout; exhale as you move toward the end of each comfortable direction.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 sets of 8–15 slow repetitions.
Expected sensation: Gentle movement and mild abdominal or hip effort are acceptable; do not force a painful end range.
Regression: Use only one direction or practise seated weight shifts.
Progression: Increase range slightly or use the motion as a warm-up for bridges, hinges or squats.
Common errors and corrections: Moving too far—make the arc smaller; gripping the buttocks—relax them; moving quickly—pause at the middle.
Evidence category: Mobility and movement confidence
Evidence strength: Stretching/mobility may help comfort, but standalone clinical benefit is uncertain.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Cat-camel through a comfortable range
Purpose: Maintain confidence with spinal flexion and extension in a supported position.
Exercise type: Mobility
Targeted musclegroups: Spinal flexors and extensors; trunk rotators
Targeted specific muscles: musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus iliopsoas
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; a bench can replace kneeling if needed.
Starting position and set-up: Place hands under or slightly in front of the shoulders and knees under the hips. Keep fingers spread and look at the floor.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Slowly round the back only as far as comfortable. 2) Return to the middle. 3) Gently lengthen the spine and allow a small arch. 4) Return to the middle and repeat.
Range and direction: Move the whole spine gradually; avoid pushing into the largest possible arch or rounding.
Breathing: Inhale toward the middle or gentle extension and exhale during the rounding phase; keep breathing easy.
Beginner dose and rest: 5–10 slow repetitions, resting as needed.
Expected sensation: A mild stretch or movement sensation is acceptable; sharp or radiating symptoms are not.
Regression: Perform the movement seated with hands on thighs or standing with hands on a wall.
Progression: Increase the range slightly, add a pause or integrate it into a warm-up.
Common errors and corrections: Dropping into the end range—slow down; moving only the neck—let the ribs and pelvis participate; holding the breath—reduce effort.
Evidence category: Spinal mobility
Evidence strength: Useful for comfortable movement; not evidence that spinal stiffness is the cause of pain.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Quadruped weight shift
Purpose: Gradually expose the shoulders, hips and trunk to supported loading.
Exercise type: Motor-control and weight-bearing
Targeted musclegroups: Shoulder girdle; hip extensors; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus serratus anterior; musculus deltoideus; musculus triceps brachii; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; sturdy bench for an elevated version.
Starting position and set-up: Start on hands and knees, with hands under the shoulders, knees under the hips and toes relaxed.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Push the floor away gently. 2) Shift your body a little toward the hands. 3) Return to the centre. 4) Shift toward the heels and then gently side to side. 5) Keep the shifts small at first.
Range and direction: Keep hands and knees in contact with the floor; use a range that stays balanced and comfortable.
Breathing: Breathe continuously, exhaling during the shift and inhaling on the return.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 30–60 seconds, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the arms, shoulders, hips or trunk is expected.
Regression: Use hands on a bench or shift only forward and back.
Progression: Increase the range, duration or add a controlled reach.
Common errors and corrections: Hands collapsing—spread the fingers; hips moving abruptly—make the shift smaller; shoulders shrugging—push away gently.
Evidence category: Supported loading and trunk control
Evidence strength: A reasonable graded activity exercise; direct evidence for this exact drill is indirect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Bird-dog, supported version
Purpose: Practise controlled movement of the hips and shoulders while the trunk remains comfortable and steady.
Exercise type: Motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Trunk stabilisers; shoulder stabilisers; hip extensors
Targeted specific muscles: musculus transversus abdominis; musculus multifidus; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus deltoideus; musculus serratus anterior
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; a wall or sturdy bench can be used for an easier version.
Starting position and set-up: Kneel on all fours with hands below or slightly in front of shoulders, knees below hips, fingers forward and eyes on the floor.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in and prepare gently. 2) Slide one foot back or lift it a few centimetres. 3) If controlled, reach the opposite hand forward. 4) Hold briefly. 5) Lower quietly and change sides.
Range and direction: Reach long rather than high; stop before the lower back arches or the pelvis twists.
Breathing: Breathe normally and exhale slowly as the limbs move; never hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 sets of 5 per side, holding 3–5 seconds, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild trunk, hip or shoulder effort is expected; sharp, electric or spreading pain is not.
Regression: Move one limb only, slide the foot or use the wall-supported version.
Progression: Hold 8–10 seconds, slow the movement or add light resistance after basic control is reliable.
Common errors and corrections: Back arching—reach lower; pelvic rotation—shorten the range; shrugging—push the floor away; rushing—pause.
Evidence category: Motor-control and trunk endurance
Evidence strength: Motor-control exercise is reasonable but this individual exercise is not uniquely validated.
Source: Saragiotto et al. 2016; Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Side plank from knees
Purpose: Build lateral trunk and hip endurance with reduced body weight.
Exercise type: Strength and endurance
Targeted musclegroups: Lateral trunk muscles; hip abductors; shoulder stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus gluteus medius; musculus gluteus minimus; musculus deltoideus; musculus triceps brachii
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; wall version if needed.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your side with knees bent, feet behind you and elbow under the shoulder. The forearm points forward and the top hand can rest on the floor.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Press the forearm into the floor. 2) Lift the hips until the shoulders, hips and knees form a comfortable line. 3) Hold. 4) Lower slowly and switch sides.
Range and direction: Use a straight line from shoulder to knee without pushing the hips far forward or backward.
Breathing: Breathe normally; exhale as you lift and continue breathing during the hold.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–4 holds of 10–20 seconds per side, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the side of the trunk and hip is expected; shoulder pain is not.
Regression: Press sideways into a wall or use a higher bench instead of the floor.
Progression: Hold longer, straighten the legs or lift the top leg after the knee version is controlled.
Common errors and corrections: Shoulder collapsing—push the floor away; hips sagging—shorten the hold; rolling backward—stack the shoulders.
Evidence category: Lateral trunk and hip endurance
Evidence strength: Reasonable strengthening option; no clear superiority over other exercise.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Full side plank
Purpose: Progress lateral trunk capacity to support carrying and unilateral tasks.
Exercise type: Strength and endurance
Targeted musclegroups: Lateral trunk muscles; hip abductors; shoulder stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus gluteus medius; musculus gluteus minimus; musculus deltoideus; musculus triceps brachii
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; optional wall or bench for regression.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your side with legs straight or knees bent. Place the elbow under the shoulder and stack the feet or stagger them.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Press the forearm down. 2) Lift the hips from the floor. 3) Keep the body in a comfortable line. 4) Hold and lower with control.
Range and direction: Use knees bent if the full lever is too demanding; do not force the hips into a perfectly straight line.
Breathing: Exhale during the lift and breathe continuously during the hold.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–4 holds of 10–30 seconds per side.
Expected sensation: Muscular effort in the side trunk, shoulder and hip is expected.
Regression: Return to the knees, wall or bench version.
Progression: Increase hold time, lift the top leg or add a controlled reach.
Common errors and corrections: Elbow too far from shoulder—move it underneath; hips sagging—shorten the hold; breath-holding—reduce the duration.
Evidence category: Lateral trunk endurance
Evidence strength: Part of progressive strengthening; not shown to be uniquely superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Front plank, incline or knees
Purpose: Build whole-trunk endurance using a modifiable body position.
Exercise type: Strength and endurance
Targeted musclegroups: Abdominal muscles; spinal extensors; shoulder girdle; hip extensors
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus deltoideus; musculus triceps brachii; musculus serratus anterior
Equipment and environment: Wall, sturdy bench or mat; choose an elevated support first.
Starting position and set-up: Place forearms or hands on a wall or bench, or use knees on a mat. Keep feet or knees behind the hips and hands below the shoulders.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Step or slide the legs back to create a straight, comfortable line. 2) Gently push the support away. 3) Hold while breathing. 4) End the hold before the back sags or shoulders collapse.
Range and direction: The body should be aligned comfortably, not rigidly frozen; a small natural curve is acceptable.
Breathing: Breathe normally; exhale while setting up and continue easy breaths during the hold.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–4 holds of 10–30 seconds, resting 30–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the abdomen, shoulders and legs is expected.
Regression: Use a higher wall or bench, or keep the knees down.
Progression: Lower the support, increase time or add a controlled limb movement.
Common errors and corrections: Back sagging—use a higher support or shorter hold; hips too high—lower slightly; shoulders shrugging—push away.
Evidence category: Whole-trunk endurance
Evidence strength: General exercise is probably beneficial; no evidence this plank is uniquely superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Glute bridge
Purpose: Strengthen hip extension and the posterior chain for walking, stairs and lifting.
Exercise type: Strength
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; deep trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus erector spinae
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; optional pillow under the head.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with knees bent, feet flat and about hip-width apart. Place heels close enough that fingertips would nearly reach them; arms rest at the sides.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Breathe in. 2) Press through both feet. 3) Lift the pelvis slowly until the hips are roughly level with the thighs, without forcing height. 4) Pause. 5) Lower slowly.
Range and direction: Move from the hips; do not chase a large back arch. Keep ribs relaxed.
Breathing: Exhale as you lift, inhale at the top and breathe out as you lower.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 8–15, resting 45–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the buttocks and back of the thighs is expected; cramping can be managed by moving the feet slightly.
Regression: Use a smaller lift or hold the pelvis only a few centimetres off the floor.
Progression: Add a 2–3-second pause, light load, marching or single-leg progression.
Common errors and corrections: Pushing through the toes—keep whole foot grounded; over-arching—lift less; knees falling together—keep them tracking over the feet.
Evidence category: Hip and posterior-chain strengthening
Evidence strength: Structured exercise is probably beneficial; the individual bridge is not uniquely superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Marching bridge
Purpose: Challenge hip extension while controlling pelvic rotation.
Exercise type: Strength and motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; hip flexors; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus iliopsoas; musculus rectus femoris; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet.
Starting position and set-up: Perform a comfortable glute bridge and keep the pelvis at a manageable height.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Shift a little weight into one foot. 2) Lift the other foot only a few centimetres. 3) Put it down quietly. 4) Repeat on the other side while keeping the bridge position.
Range and direction: Use a small step; the pelvis should not drop or twist to lift the foot.
Breathing: Breathe normally; exhale as one foot lifts and inhale as it returns.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 5–10 per side, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the buttocks and trunk is expected; cramping or sharp symptoms mean regress.
Regression: Return to a two-leg bridge or use alternating heel lifts without fully lifting the foot.
Progression: Increase the hold, use a slower lift or add light external load.
Common errors and corrections: Pelvis rocking—lower the bridge; knee drifting outward—increase foot pressure evenly; rushing—pause after each foot lift.
Evidence category: Hip strength and trunk control
Evidence strength: A reasonable progression within strengthening; direct evidence for this exact variation is indirect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Hip-hinge drill
Purpose: Practise bending and lifting with the hips and legs while allowing a natural spinal position.
Exercise type: Functional motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus transversus abdominis
Equipment and environment: Wall, chair or dowel; clear floor space.
Starting position and set-up: Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees softly unlocked, and a wall about 10–15 cm behind the hips. Arms can cross over the chest or reach forward.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Keep the feet planted. 2) Push the hips backward toward the wall. 3) Let the trunk lean forward naturally. 4) Touch the wall with the hips if comfortable. 5) Push the feet into the floor and stand tall.
Range and direction: The hips travel backward and the knees bend slightly; do not force the back to remain perfectly straight.
Breathing: Inhale while lowering or hinging and exhale as you stand; do not hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 6–12 repetitions, resting 45–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the buttocks and thighs is expected; a comfortable back stretch can be acceptable but sharp pain is not.
Regression: Use a higher target, smaller range or practise seated weight shifts.
Progression: Hold a light object close to the body, lower the target or increase load gradually.
Common errors and corrections: Squatting straight down—send hips backward; knees locking—soften them; neck craning—look at the floor several metres ahead.
Evidence category: Functional lifting and posterior-chain strengthening
Evidence strength: Progressive strengthening is supported; no single lifting pattern is mandatory.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al.; McGill for loading context.
Name: Sit-to-stand
Purpose: Improve functional leg and hip strength for chairs, toilets and daily transitions.
Exercise type: Strength and functional
Targeted musclegroups: Quadriceps; hip extensors; hamstrings; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus erector spinae; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis
Equipment and environment: A sturdy chair that will not slide; optional armrests or wall nearby.
Starting position and set-up: Place the chair against a wall. Sit near the front with feet flat, about hip-width apart, and toes pointing mostly forward. Lean the trunk slightly forward.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Move the nose over the toes. 2) Press through the feet and stand. 3) Pause upright without locking the knees. 4) Push the hips backward and lower slowly until seated.
Range and direction: Use a depth that is comfortable; the trunk may lean forward naturally.
Breathing: Exhale while standing and inhale while lowering; breathe continuously.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 6–12, 2–3 days per week, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Effort in thighs and buttocks is expected; use hands if balance or strength is limited.
Regression: Use a higher chair, arm support or partial stand.
Progression: Lower the chair, slow the descent, add a light load or use a staggered stance.
Common errors and corrections: Knees collapsing inward—aim them toward the second toe; dropping into the chair—slow the descent; heels lifting—move feet slightly back.
Evidence category: Functional lower-body strengthening
Evidence strength: Supported by the broader exercise evidence; this exact exercise is a practical functional choice.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Squat to box
Purpose: Build lower-body capacity with a consistent depth target.
Exercise type: Strength and functional
Targeted musclegroups: Quadriceps; hip extensors; hamstrings; calf muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus soleus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus erector spinae; musculus transversus abdominis
Equipment and environment: A sturdy box, bench or chair against a wall; optional light weight.
Starting position and set-up: Stand facing away from the box with feet about shoulder-width apart and toes comfortable. Keep the box close enough to touch without falling backward.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Reach the hips backward. 2) Bend the knees and lower toward the box. 3) Touch or lightly sit without collapsing. 4) Press through the feet to stand.
Range and direction: Let the trunk incline naturally and keep the knees tracking in the same general direction as the toes.
Breathing: Inhale while lowering and exhale while standing; do not hold the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 6–12, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the thighs, hips and trunk is expected.
Regression: Use a higher box, reduce depth or hold a support.
Progression: Lower the box, add load, slow the lowering phase or use a staggered stance.
Common errors and corrections: Knees cave inward—reduce depth and track them over the feet; dropping—control the descent; weight on toes—keep the whole foot down.
Evidence category: Functional strengthening
Evidence strength: General strengthening is probably beneficial; no evidence this squat variation is uniquely superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Split squat
Purpose: Develop single-leg strength, balance and hip control.
Exercise type: Strength and balance
Targeted musclegroups: Quadriceps; hip extensors; hip abductors; hamstrings; calf muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus gluteus minimus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis
Equipment and environment: Wall, rail or chair for support; optional dumbbells later.
Starting position and set-up: Stand in a short staggered stance with one foot in front and one behind, feet about hip-width side to side, not on a tight line. Hold the support lightly.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Keep most weight through the front foot. 2) Bend both knees and lower a short distance. 3) Keep the front heel down. 4) Press through the front foot to return. 5) Complete the set before changing sides.
Range and direction: Lower vertically within a comfortable range; the front knee may travel forward as long as it tracks comfortably.
Breathing: Inhale down and exhale up; use the support for balance rather than pulling yourself upward.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 5–10 per side, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Effort in the front thigh and buttock is expected; balance difficulty is a reason to use more support.
Regression: Use a shorter range, hold the support with both hands or practise a static stance.
Progression: Increase depth, add load, slow the lowering phase or elevate the rear foot only when ready.
Common errors and corrections: Front knee collapsing—aim toward the second toe; feet too narrow—widen the stance; pushing from the back foot—shift weight forward.
Evidence category: Unilateral lower-body strengthening
Evidence strength: Reasonable strengthening option; no proven superiority over other strengthening.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Step-up
Purpose: Train leg strength and controlled stair movement.
Exercise type: Strength and functional
Targeted musclegroups: Quadriceps; hip extensors; hamstrings; calf muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus; musculus tibialis anterior; musculus transversus abdominis
Equipment and environment: A low, stable step next to a rail or wall; clear space around it.
Starting position and set-up: Stand close to the step with feet hip-width apart. Place the whole front foot on the centre of the step and keep a hand near support.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Lean slightly forward from the ankles. 2) Press through the foot on the step to rise. 3) Bring the other foot up if needed. 4) Step down slowly and repeat on the same side or alternate.
Range and direction: Use a step height that lets the knee and hip move comfortably; do not jump or push excessively from the trailing foot.
Breathing: Exhale while stepping up and inhale while stepping down.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 6–12 per side, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Thigh, hip and calf effort is expected; wobbling or knee pain means reduce height.
Regression: Use a lower step, hold the rail or practise a weight shift onto the step.
Progression: Increase height, reduce hand support, add light load or slow the descent.
Common errors and corrections: Trailing leg doing all the work—keep it light; knee collapsing—track it over the foot; stepping down quickly—slow the lowering.
Evidence category: Functional leg strength and conditioning
Evidence strength: A reasonable functional strengthening exercise; direct evidence for this exact height or dose is indirect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Romanian deadlift pattern
Purpose: Progress hip-hinge strength and tolerance for lifting a load.
Exercise type: Strength
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; adductors; spinal extensors; grip and upper-back stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus trapezius; musculus latissimus dorsi; musculi flexores digitorum
Equipment and environment: Two light dumbbells, kettlebell or household objects; open floor space.
Starting position and set-up: Stand with feet hip-width apart and the weights close to the thighs. Keep knees softly bent, shoulders relaxed and the load close.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Push the hips backward. 2) Let the weights slide down the thighs while the trunk leans forward. 3) Stop when the hamstrings are gently loaded or before the back rounds uncomfortably. 4) Press the feet down and bring the hips forward to stand.
Range and direction: The weights travel close to the legs; range is limited by comfortable hip motion, not by reaching the floor.
Breathing: Inhale during the hinge and exhale as you stand; do not hold the breath for a light beginner load.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 6–12, resting 90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the hamstrings, buttocks and back is expected; sharp or spreading symptoms are not.
Regression: Use a dowel, empty hands or start from an elevated surface.
Progression: Increase load gradually, lower the starting height, slow the descent or progress to a unilateral version.
Common errors and corrections: Squatting instead of hinging—send hips backward; load drifting away—keep it close; rounding at the bottom—shorten range.
Evidence category: Posterior-chain strengthening and lifting tolerance
Evidence strength: Progressive resistance exercise is a reasonable option; no exact load is established as optimal.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Arora et al. 2026; McGill for loading context.
Name: Hip thrust
Purpose: Progress hip-extension strength using a supported upper back.
Exercise type: Strength
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; adductors; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis
Equipment and environment: Stable bench against a wall or a floor-mat bridge; optional padded light weight.
Starting position and set-up: Sit on the floor with the upper back against the bench edge, feet flat and knees bent. Place the bench below the shoulder blades, not the neck.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Tuck the chin slightly and keep the ribs comfortable. 2) Press through both feet. 3) Lift the hips until the trunk is roughly level with the thighs. 4) Pause gently. 5) Lower under control.
Range and direction: Use a height that does not force the lower back into a large arch; the movement should come mainly from the hips.
Breathing: Exhale while lifting and inhale while lowering; breathe continuously.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–4 sets of 6–12, resting 90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild buttock and thigh effort is expected; neck pressure or pinching is not.
Regression: Use a floor bridge or a lower support.
Progression: Add a pause, light load, greater control or a single-leg variation.
Common errors and corrections: Bench too high—lower the support; head pushed backward—keep chin slightly tucked; over-arching—lift less.
Evidence category: Hip extension strengthening
Evidence strength: A practical progressive strengthening option; the individual exercise is not uniquely supported.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Pallof press
Purpose: Practise resisting rotation while the arms move.
Exercise type: Strength and anti-rotation
Targeted musclegroups: Abdominal muscles; spinal stabilisers; shoulder and hip stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus rectus abdominis; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus gluteus medius; musculus deltoideus; musculus pectoralis major; musculus triceps brachii
Equipment and environment: Resistance band or cable securely anchored at chest height; open space.
Starting position and set-up: Stand sideways to the anchor, far enough away that the band has light tension. Hold the handle with both hands at the centre of the chest, feet hip-width apart and knees soft.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Brace gently. 2) Press the hands straight forward until the elbows are almost straight. 3) Pause without turning toward the anchor. 4) Bring the hands back to the chest. 5) Turn around and repeat on the other side.
Range and direction: Keep the chest and pelvis facing forward; a small natural adjustment is acceptable but do not fight rotation maximally.
Breathing: Exhale as the hands press away and inhale as they return.
Beginner dose and rest: 2–3 sets of 6–12 per side or 10–20-second holds, resting 45–60 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the trunk and shoulders is expected; shoulder or back pain is not.
Regression: Use a lighter band, stand closer to the anchor or hold the band at the chest without pressing.
Progression: Step farther away, use a split stance or add slow stepping after the basic press is controlled.
Common errors and corrections: Turning toward the anchor—use less tension; shoulders shrugging—lower them; elbows locking—keep a soft bend.
Evidence category: Anti-rotation trunk strengthening
Evidence strength: A reasonable strengthening variation; no evidence this exercise is superior to other trunk work.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Suitcase carry
Purpose: Build lateral trunk, grip and walking capacity with one-sided loading.
Exercise type: Strength and loaded carry
Targeted musclegroups: Lateral trunk; hip stabilisers; grip; shoulder girdle; lower limbs
Targeted specific muscles: musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus trapezius; musculus deltoideus; musculi flexores digitorum; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus quadriceps femoris; musculus biceps femoris; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus
Equipment and environment: One manageable dumbbell, kettlebell or household bag; clear, level walking path.
Starting position and set-up: Stand tall with the weight in one hand. Place the other hand on the hip or let it hang. Keep feet hip-width apart and the weight close to the thigh.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Take a breath and gently prepare the trunk. 2) Walk slowly for the planned distance. 3) Turn carefully. 4) Stop, set the weight down safely and change hands.
Range and direction: Do not lean toward or away from the weight; allow a small natural adjustment.
Breathing: Breathe normally while walking; do not hold the breath to stay upright.
Beginner dose and rest: 3–6 carries of 20–40 metres or 20–40 seconds per side, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the hand, shoulder, side trunk and legs is expected.
Regression: Use a lighter object, shorter distance or a supported standing hold.
Progression: Increase distance before load, then add load or use a more demanding walking route.
Common errors and corrections: Leaning—use less load; shoulder hiking—relax it; rushing—shorten the steps and slow down.
Evidence category: Loaded carry and lateral trunk capacity
Evidence strength: A practical progressive exercise; direct evidence for this exact carry is indirect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al.; McGill for loading context.
Name: Farmer carry
Purpose: Build whole-body loading and walking tolerance with balanced loads.
Exercise type: Strength and loaded carry
Targeted musclegroups: Grip; shoulder girdle; spinal stabilisers; hips and legs
Targeted specific muscles: musculus trapezius; musculus deltoideus; musculus biceps brachii; musculus triceps brachii; musculi flexores digitorum; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus gluteus maximus; musculus quadriceps femoris; musculus biceps femoris; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus
Equipment and environment: Two light dumbbells, kettlebells or bags; level, unobstructed path.
Starting position and set-up: Stand with one weight in each hand, arms by the sides, feet hip-width apart and shoulders relaxed.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Lift the weights using a hip hinge and keep them close. 2) Stand tall without leaning. 3) Walk at a controlled pace. 4) Stop before grip or posture fails and lower the weights by hinging.
Range and direction: Keep ribs and pelvis comfortable; do not force the shoulders back or arch the lower back.
Breathing: Breathe normally and avoid breath-holding.
Beginner dose and rest: 3–6 carries of 20–40 metres, resting 60–90 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild grip, shoulder, trunk and leg effort is expected.
Regression: Use lighter loads, shorter carries or hold one object close to the chest.
Progression: Increase distance, then load, or introduce gentle changes of direction.
Common errors and corrections: Shrugging—let shoulders hang; dropping weights—stop earlier; leaning back—reduce load.
Evidence category: Loaded carry and general conditioning
Evidence strength: Reasonable whole-body strengthening; no specific carry is proven superior.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Hip-flexor mobility
Purpose: Improve comfortable hip-extension tolerance without forcing the lower back.
Exercise type: Mobility and stretching
Targeted musclegroups: Hip flexors; anterior thigh; hip extensors
Targeted specific muscles: musculus iliopsoas; musculus rectus femoris; musculus sartorius; musculus tensor fasciae latae; musculus gluteus maximus
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; wall or chair for balance.
Starting position and set-up: Kneel on one knee with the other foot in front, or stand in a short split stance. Keep the torso tall and hold a support if balancing.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Gently tighten the buttock of the kneeling-side leg. 2) Move the pelvis forward a small amount while keeping the ribs over the pelvis. 3) Pause at a mild stretch in the front of the hip. 4) Return and relax.
Range and direction: The stretch comes from the hip, not from arching the lower back; shorten the stance if needed.
Breathing: Breathe slowly; exhale as you ease forward and continue breathing during the hold.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 holds of 20–30 seconds per side or 6–10 slow repetitions.
Expected sensation: A mild front-of-hip stretch is expected; pinching, sharp pain or back compression is not.
Regression: Use standing support, a shorter stance or no forward shift.
Progression: Increase the range slightly, add a gentle arm reach or use a half-kneeling variation with better balance.
Common errors and corrections: Arching the back—tighten the rear buttock and reduce the shift; twisting—keep the hip bones facing forward; bouncing—hold still.
Evidence category: Hip mobility and comfort
Evidence strength: May help mobility or comfort; stretching alone has uncertain clinical benefit.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et. al. for technique.
Name: Hamstring stretch
Purpose: Improve comfortable posterior-leg mobility when it helps movement or preparation.
Exercise type: Mobility and stretching
Targeted musclegroups: Hamstrings; calf muscles
Targeted specific muscles: musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus
Equipment and environment: Chair, wall or strap; mat for a supine version.
Starting position and set-up: For a supported standing version, place one heel on a low step with the knee slightly bent and hold a support. Keep the other foot flat.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Keep the chest relaxed. 2) Hinge slightly at the hips until a mild stretch is felt behind the thigh. 3) Hold without bouncing. 4) Return by bending the supported knee.
Range and direction: A mild stretch is enough; do not pull the toes aggressively or round the back to chase more range.
Breathing: Breathe slowly and exhale as you settle into the stretch.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 holds of 20–30 seconds per side, resting between sides.
Expected sensation: A mild, broad stretch behind the thigh is expected; tingling, burning or electric symptoms are not.
Regression: Use a lower support, keep the knee more bent or perform the stretch lying with a strap.
Progression: Gradually increase range or use active leg movements rather than a harder forced stretch.
Common errors and corrections: Locking the knee—soften it; rounding the back—hinge less; bouncing—hold a steady position.
Evidence category: Mobility and stretching
Evidence strength: Reasonable adjunct for comfort or range; not established as a standalone back-pain treatment.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Gluteal stretch
Purpose: Improve hip comfort and mobility without forcing a painful spinal position.
Exercise type: Mobility and stretching
Targeted musclegroups: Gluteal muscles; deep external hip rotators
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus gluteus minimus; musculus piriformis; musculus obturator internus; musculus gemellus superior; musculus gemellus inferior; musculus quadratus femoris
Equipment and environment: Mat or firm bed; optional strap.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your back with both knees bent. Cross one ankle over the opposite thigh, or use a seated figure-four with both feet supported.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Keep the crossed foot relaxed. 2) Draw the supporting thigh toward you only until a mild buttock stretch is felt. 3) Hold while breathing. 4) Lower slowly and change sides.
Range and direction: Keep the pelvis comfortable and do not pull the knee aggressively toward the opposite shoulder.
Breathing: Breathe slowly; exhale as the leg moves toward the stretch and continue relaxed breaths.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 holds of 20–30 seconds per side.
Expected sensation: A mild stretch in the buttock or outer hip is expected; groin pain or nerve-like symptoms are not.
Regression: Keep the supporting foot on the floor or use a seated version with less range.
Progression: Increase range slightly or use active hip rotations after the static hold.
Common errors and corrections: Pulling too hard—use less force; pelvis twisting—keep both hip bones heavy; rounding the neck—support the head.
Evidence category: Hip mobility and comfort
Evidence strength: Adjunctive mobility option; direct evidence for this exact stretch is limited.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Thoracic rotation
Purpose: Improve upper-back rotation so ordinary reaching does not rely entirely on the lower back.
Exercise type: Mobility and motor-control
Targeted musclegroups: Thoracic rotators; spinal stabilisers; shoulder girdle
Targeted specific muscles: musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus multifidus; musculus rotatores; musculus semispinalis thoracis; musculus erector spinae; musculus serratus anterior
Equipment and environment: Mat or carpet; pillow for head support.
Starting position and set-up: Lie on your side with hips and knees bent and arms straight in front at chest height. Place the head on a pillow so the neck is comfortable.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Keep the knees together. 2) Slowly sweep the top arm in an arc toward the floor behind you. 3) Rotate through the upper back only as far as comfortable. 4) Return the arm to the start and repeat.
Range and direction: The knees stay mostly together while the upper ribs rotate; do not force the hand to the floor.
Breathing: Inhale as the arm opens and exhale as it returns, or use any natural breathing rhythm.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 sets of 5–10 per side, moving slowly.
Expected sensation: A mild stretch across the chest or upper back is expected; sharp lower-back symptoms are not.
Regression: Use a smaller arc or perform a seated rotation with hands across the chest.
Progression: Increase the arc, add a reach or perform the movement in a half-kneeling position.
Common errors and corrections: Knees separating—use a pillow between them; neck turning first—keep eyes following the hand gently; forcing range—stop earlier.
Evidence category: Thoracic mobility
Evidence strength: Mobility may support comfortable function; no evidence it corrects a specific cause of low-back pain.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Comfortable trunk rotation
Purpose: Maintain confidence with ordinary spinal rotation in a pain-tolerated range.
Exercise type: Mobility
Targeted musclegroups: Trunk rotators; spinal stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus multifidus; musculus rotatores; musculus erector spinae; musculus quadratus lumborum
Equipment and environment: Chair or mat; clear space.
Starting position and set-up: Sit near the front of a stable chair with feet flat, or stand with feet hip-width apart. Cross the arms lightly over the chest.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Turn the chest and shoulders slowly to one side. 2) Stop at a comfortable range. 3) Return to centre. 4) Repeat to the other side without bouncing.
Range and direction: Let the pelvis stay mostly forward but allow small natural movement; do not pin it rigidly.
Breathing: Breathe out during the turn and in as you return, without holding the breath.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–2 sets of 5–10 per side.
Expected sensation: A mild movement or stretch sensation is acceptable; sharp, radiating or escalating symptoms are not.
Regression: Use a smaller range, turn from a higher chair or practise only one direction that is comfortable.
Progression: Integrate rotation into reaching, stepping or a light task-specific lift.
Common errors and corrections: Moving only the neck—turn the chest; bouncing—slow down; gripping the chair—use less force.
Evidence category: Spinal mobility and movement confidence
Evidence strength: A reasonable comfort and exposure exercise; stretching/mobility alone has uncertain treatment effect.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Kisner et al. for technique.
Name: Walking
Purpose: Build aerobic capacity, activity tolerance and confidence with a low-cost whole-body activity.
Exercise type: Aerobic
Targeted musclegroups: Hip muscles; thigh muscles; calf muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus iliopsoas; musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus; musculus tibialis anterior; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus erector spinae
Equipment and environment: Comfortable shoes and a level, safe route; a treadmill is optional.
Starting position and set-up: Start with a route close to home or a place where you can rest. Stand tall but relaxed and choose a pace at which you can speak in sentences.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Walk at the planned pace. 2) Let the arms swing naturally. 3) Turn before fatigue changes your gait. 4) Finish with an easy minute rather than stopping abruptly after a hard effort.
Range and direction: Use a comfortable stride; do not force a particular posture or stride length.
Breathing: Breathe naturally; the talk test is a practical guide to moderate intensity.
Beginner dose and rest: Start with 5–10 minutes, 4–6 days per week; add 2–5 minutes every several days if recovery is acceptable, aiming toward 20–30 minutes on 3–5 days per week.
Expected sensation: Mild muscular effort and temporary local discomfort can be acceptable; a new limp or escalating leg symptoms are not.
Regression: Use shorter bouts, slower pace, flat ground, cycling or pool exercise.
Progression: Increase duration before speed; later add gentle hills or intervals if desired.
Common errors and corrections: Increasing time and speed together—change one variable; overstriding—shorten the steps; ignoring a limp—stop and reassess.
Evidence category: Aerobic activity and general conditioning
Evidence strength: Structured exercise probably improves pain and function; walking has stronger evidence for recurrence prevention than treatment of established chronic pain.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; Pocovi et al. 2024 WalkBack; WHO 2023.
Name: Cycling or pool exercise
Purpose: Provide an alternative aerobic activity when walking or impact is less comfortable.
Exercise type: Aerobic
Targeted musclegroups: Hip muscles; thigh muscles; calf muscles; trunk stabilisers
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus gluteus medius; musculus iliopsoas; musculus sartorius; musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus gastrocnemius; musculus soleus; musculus tibialis anterior; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus erector spinae
Equipment and environment: Stationary or outdoor bicycle, or access to a safe pool; use appropriate safety equipment.
Starting position and set-up: For cycling, adjust the seat so the knee remains slightly bent at the bottom of the pedal stroke. For pool exercise, use a depth where you can stand securely and exit safely.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Begin at an easy pace. 2) Keep the shoulders relaxed. 3) Continue for the planned time. 4) Reduce the pace gradually before stopping.
Range and direction: Choose a position that does not force painful rounding or twisting; adjust the bicycle or use water support as needed.
Breathing: Breathe naturally and keep the effort low enough to speak in short sentences.
Beginner dose and rest: Start with 5–15 minutes at comfortable intensity, 2–5 days per week; increase duration before intensity.
Expected sensation: Mild general exertion is expected; sustained worsening from the position or repetitive motion means change the setup or activity.
Regression: Shorter intervals, lower resistance, more upright cycling or gentle pool walking.
Progression: Increase total time, then resistance or pace, one change at a time.
Common errors and corrections: Resistance too high—reduce it; seat too low—raise it; holding the breath—lower intensity; unsafe pool entry—use supervision.
Evidence category: Aerobic conditioning
Evidence strength: A reasonable exercise alternative; individual modality superiority is not established.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; WHO 2023; Kisner et al. for exercise programming.
Name: Progressive lifting from an elevated surface
Purpose: Restore confidence and capacity for household, work or training-related lifting.
Exercise type: Strength and functional graded exposure
Targeted musclegroups: Hip extensors; hamstrings; quadriceps; spinal stabilisers; upper-back and grip muscles
Targeted specific muscles: musculus gluteus maximus; musculus biceps femoris; musculus semitendinosus; musculus semimembranosus; musculus adductor magnus; musculus rectus femoris; musculus vastus lateralis; musculus vastus medialis; musculus vastus intermedius; musculus erector spinae; musculus multifidus; musculus quadratus lumborum; musculus transversus abdominis; musculus obliquus externus abdominis; musculus obliquus internus abdominis; musculus trapezius; musculus latissimus dorsi; musculi flexores digitorum
Equipment and environment: A stable table or bench, a light object with handles and clear floor space; a spotter can help with unfamiliar loads.
Starting position and set-up: Place the object on a surface around mid-thigh to waist height. Stand close with feet hip-width apart, the object between or just in front of the feet, and choose a comfortable stance.
Step-by-step movement: 1) Move close to the object. 2) Bend the knees and/or hinge at the hips. 3) Place both hands securely around it. 4) Keep it close as you stand by pushing through the feet. 5) Walk only if needed. 6) Lower it by reversing the movement, without dropping it.
Range and direction: Use a natural, comfortable back position; the object should travel close to the body and the range should be limited by control, not fear of ordinary spinal movement.
Breathing: Inhale before the lift and exhale as you stand for a light load; do not hold the breath for prolonged periods.
Beginner dose and rest: 1–3 sets of 5–10 repetitions with a light load, resting 60–120 seconds.
Expected sensation: Mild effort in the legs, hips, arms and trunk is expected; sharp or spreading symptoms are not.
Regression: Use a lighter object, higher surface, shorter distance or practise the hip hinge without a load.
Progression: Lower the surface gradually, increase load in small steps, carry farther or practise the exact work/sport task.
Common errors and corrections: Load too far away—step closer; twisting while lifting—turn with the feet; rounding or bracing excessively—use a smaller load and breathe; dropping the object—stop earlier.
Evidence category: Functional strengthening and graded exposure
Evidence strength: Progressive exercise and activity are supported; no single lifting technique is proven uniquely protective.
Source: Verville et al. 2023; WHO 2023; McGill for loading context.
